title: Intel Just Had Its Best Quarter in 15 Years. The Stock Fell 29% in July.
subtitle: A 92% EPS beat, 18A output up 50% quarter-over-quarter, and a $20B capex commitment — so why did Wall Street sell the news?
summary: Intel delivered its fastest revenue growth in 15 years and a 92% EPS beat in Q2 2026 — yet the stock fell roughly 29% in July as a non-cash $12.5B mark-to-market on the government's CHIPS Act escrowed shares drowned out the real story. Behind the GAAP noise: DCAI up 59%, 18A output running 25% above target, and a raised $20B-plus capex commitment that signals genuine customer conviction.

bodyHtml:
Intel just reported its best quarter in fifteen years, and the stock spent July getting wrecked anyway. That disconnect is the whole story, and it's worth understanding.

Let's start with the numbers, because they're genuinely good. Revenue came in at $16.1 billion, up 25% year over year — the fastest growth Intel has posted since the third quarter of 2011. Non-GAAP EPS was $0.42 against a consensus of $0.22 — a 92% beat, nearly double the estimate. Non-GAAP gross margin hit 41.8%, 280 basis points above guidance. Operating cash flow reached $7.0 billion, free cash flow was positive at $4.45 billion, and the company beat its own guidance for the seventh consecutive quarter.

So why did the stock fall roughly 29% in July? Start with the headline GAAP number, which showed a massive loss. That loss is almost entirely a non-cash mark-to-market on the government's CHIPS Act escrowed shares — a $12.5 billion charge that exists only on paper. No cash left the building. The U.S. government owns roughly 10% of Intel in non-voting shares with no board seat, and the escrow structure forces quarterly mark-to-market swings unrelated to how the business is actually running. It's noise. Loud, ugly, headline-generating noise.

The business underneath is the real story, and it's accelerating. Data center and AI revenue hit $6.3 billion, up 59% year over year and 24% sequentially — a company catching the AI wave, not watching it pass. Client computing did $8.9 billion, up 13%. And Intel Foundry, the division that was supposed to be the hardest part of the turnaround, grew 31% to $5.8 billion with external revenue up 68%. Roughly 70% of Intel's revenue now comes from AI-driven businesses, and that chunk grew more than 70% year over year. The mix shift is real and fast.

Then there's the technology roadmap, where the skeptics have lived for the better part of a decade. 18A output is running about 25% above target and up more than 50% sequentially, with yields ahead of expectations. 18A-P has entered risk production. And here's the genuinely surprising part: 14A is reportedly showing defect density and transistor performance that outpace 18A's early trajectory, with the PDK due in October, risk production in the second half of next year, and high-volume manufacturing in 2028. If that holds, Intel's roadmap isn't just repaired — it's competitive at the leading edge again. Custom ASIC work is already at a roughly $2 billion run rate with a target around $4 billion.

Here's the tell that the confidence is real: capex guidance was raised to more than $20 billion for 2026, with 2027 significantly higher. Nobody commits capital like that on hope. That's customer demand with committed orders behind it.

The balance sheet can absorb all of it. Cash and short-term investments sit at $29.7 billion against $50.5 billion of total debt — net debt of about $20.8 billion, manageable given $7 billion a quarter in operating cash flow. The government's stake is a political overhang, but it's non-voting and holds no board seat: a patient capital partner, not a puppet master.

The stock context matters here. Intel shares more than doubled off the start of the year before July, then got caught in a semiconductor-wide selloff that knocked the whole sector down roughly 19% from its June peak. Intel fell further than the group — about 29% — and even a strong report couldn't hold the bounce: the stock popped after hours, then faded about 8% the next day as the GAAP headline did its damage. It has since rebounded from the July lows. The analyst crowd is split: of the analysts covering the stock, 14 rate it Buy or Strong Buy, most say Hold, and three are negative. The forward multiple on 2027 estimates is elevated — the market is paying up for a turnaround that isn't finished yet.

CEO Lip-Bu Tan framed it plainly: "AI is driving unprecedented demand for compute... our Q2 results represent our strongest revenue growth in more than fifteen years, enabled by greater speed, accountability, and customer focus."

So is the July selloff a buying opportunity or a warning? The honest answer: the fundamentals made a decisive turn, and the market's reaction was driven by accounting noise and sector-wide de-risking. But Intel has burned investors at exactly this point in the cycle before, and the valuation now assumes the roadmap delivers. If 14A comes in on schedule and the foundry's external business keeps compounding, July will look like a gift. If the roadmap slips again, the stock has a long way to fall from an already-rich multiple. The quarter was real. The question is whether the next two years look like the next two quarters.

Disclosure: The Signal holds no position in INTC. Positions may change. This is not financial advice.
